passage:
Every evening on the school steps in Sultanpur, Nikita told anyone who would listen, "I'm going to fail physics. I'll get maybe twenty." Her friend Ramesh raised an eyebrow. "You haven't opened chapter six." "What's the point? If I expect the worst, I won't be sad." She shut the book and picked at her nails.
On result day she got sixty-four. "See?" she said, grinning with relief. "Lucky. I expected twenty."
Ramesh walked with her in silence. Then he said, "You skipped half the syllabus because you'd decided you'd fail. What would you have got if you hadn't?"
Nikita's smile faltered. "I don't know," she said. "I never found out."

qa.q: What mark did Nikita expect to get in physics?
What was Nikita feeling when she said that if she expects the worst she won't be sad?
qa.a: Nikita was afraid of disappointment and protecting herself from it, so she lowered her expectations as a shield.

qa.q: What could Nikita try before the next exam?
qa.a: Nikita could open chapter six and work one topic a day, while still expecting some nerves. Studying first would let her find out what her real result could be.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Nikita's habit of predicting failure?
qa.a: Ramesh seems to see that it quietly cuts her effort, since she skipped half the syllabus. He asks what she might have got if she had tried.

grounding: A teenager expects the worst on every exam so any result feels like a win, though it quietly reduces effort.

passage:
The night before the history exam, Leila wrote FAIL, FAIL, MAYBE PASS on the back of her hand. "Realistically, I'll get a D," she told Hiroshi over the video call. "That way any grade is good news." She spent the evening on the first two topics, then scrolled her phone.
Hiroshi rubbed his eyes on the screen. "You haven't touched the last three."
"Because I'll fail anyway."
"You say that every time. And every time you got a B."
Leila looked at the words on her hand. She hadn't thought of it that way. Slowly she pulled the textbook closer. "One more hour," she said. "Just the third topic."
Hiroshi grinned. "I'll read mine at the same time."

qa.q: What did Leila write on the back of her hand?
qa.a: Leila wrote FAIL, FAIL, MAYBE PASS on the back of her hand.

qa.q: Why does Leila say she will get a D?
qa.a: Leila is anxious about being disappointed, so expecting the worst is a shield: any grade then feels like good news.

qa.q: What small step did Leila take after the video call?
qa.a: Leila agreed to study one more hour on the third topic, with Hiroshi reading his notes at the same time.

qa.q: What might Hiroshi have been thinking as he pointed out the B grades?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably thought that Leila's predictions were not matching her real results, and wanted to nudge her without lecturing.

grounding: A teenager expects the worst before exams so any result feels like a win, which can quietly reduce effort.
